CNBC Oracle shares jumped on Wednesday after the software company issued a revenue forecast of $225 billion for fiscal 2030, implying 35% average annual growth, and said it will limit additional fundraising over that stretch to $20 billion. At its investor day, Oracle said that as part of its financing plan for fiscal 2027 through 2030, the amount raised will be divided equally between equity and debt. "Vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments are expected to reduce upfront cash requirements through the transition to positive free cash flow," Oracle said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Analysts polled by LSEG expected revenue growth of 8% in fiscal 2027, followed by significant acceleration over the next two years. They're projecting revenue in fiscal 2030 of $224.2 billion. Prior to Wednesday, Oracle had lost about one-third of its value this year on concern that rising interest rates and the company's hefty debt load will make its artificial intelligence buildout too costly. Oracle has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P. Long known as a giant in enterprise software, Oracle jumped into the AI infrastructure game in a major way last year to try and compete with the hyperscalers like Google and Amazon . Its capital expenditures more than doubled to $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and are expected to jump another 65% this fiscal year to $91.9 billion, according to FactSet. Oracle needs revenue expansion from its buildout to cover the soaring costs. The company said its operating margin in fiscal 2030 will top 40%. Oracle also said said it will turn free cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and reach more than $30 billion in free cash flow the following year. Analysts expect negative free cash flow of $35 billion this fiscal year and a similar number next year. —CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report. This is breaking news. headlines.article_text: FTC demands Walmart and others hand over data on personalized pricing Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Andrew Ferguson speaks during the Semafor World Economy Summit 2025 at Conrad Washington on April 23, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kayla Bartkowski | Getty Images The Federal Trade Commission is demanding information from Walmart , Uber and seven other companies on whether and how they use consumers' personal data such as location, browsing history and income to set individual prices, wages and job offers, a senior FTC official told Reuters on Wednesday. The FTC is flexing its consumer protection powers ahead of the U.S. congressional elections next week, as voters consistently rank the cost of living as the most important issue. Target , along with app services Lyft , DoorDash and Instacart, and airlines Delta , United , JetBlue , are also receiving demands, the official said. The FTC will use the information to eventually publish a study to help inform regulators and lawmakers about personalized pricing and wage setting practices. The advance of algorithmic pricing technology, including tools that incorporate AI, has fueled concern that companies are able to set prices for shoppers on an individual basis in order to extract the maximum price each shopper would be willing to pay. Personalized pricing strategies are difficult to observe from the outside, because they serve different prices to different people. The FTC study aims to fill in that knowledge gap, demanding comprehensive information about the tools, strategies, and data companies use as well as how they affect prices, wages and job offers. Efforts by state lawmakers to ban personalized pricing, along with the use of algorithms to individually tailor wages, have taken off in recent years. The National Retail Federation has criticized the laws and defended retailers' use of data-driven discounts as a means of incentivizing loyalty. FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson has said personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws where consumers do not expect it and that companies should expect enforcement. After the FTC called for public comment, hundreds of commenters urged the FTC to ban the practice outright. The FTC has said it does not have the authority to issue a blanket prohibition against the practice.
